Chapter 2: How Situations Shape Choices and Actions
Picture this for a second—a workplace where the boss is barely around, but the rules? They’re strict, and everyone’s expected to deliver. New folks come in, full of enthusiasm and ready to follow the handbook. But pretty soon, they start to notice something: shortcuts are everywhere, and speaking up about issues is quietly discouraged. What happens next? Even the most well-meaning people start to bend the rules, just to keep up... or to stay out of trouble.
It’s not like they suddenly became different people overnight. Instead, the situation slowly nudged them, step by step, into making choices they probably wouldn’t have made on their own.
And honestly, this kind of pattern pops up in all sorts of places—schools, offices, even inside families. What’s going on around us—what gets rewarded, what’s punished, and what simply gets ignored—can have a huge effect on how we act. Most of the time, we don’t even notice the shift as it’s happening. It’s only when we look back that we realize just how much we’ve changed.
There’s a powerful example from psychology that really brings this to life. Maybe you’ve heard of it—a famous study where volunteers were asked to play the roles of guards and prisoners in a pretend jail. The guards got uniforms, sunglasses, and the power to enforce the rules. The prisoners? They were given smocks, numbers, and told to follow orders.
Within days, the guards started acting harshly, inventing punishments, even humiliating the prisoners. And the prisoners? They became passive and withdrawn. Things got so intense, the researchers had to end the experiment early because it was spiraling out of control.
What’s really striking isn’t just what people did—but how fast it happened. The guards weren’t picked because they were aggressive, and the prisoners weren’t chosen for being quiet or meek. It was the roles and the environment that did most of the work.
So, what’s the takeaway? Situations can bring out sides of us we might not even know are there.
And it doesn’t just happen in experiments. In real life, people get shaped by the roles they’re handed and the expectations around them all the time. Think about a teacher pressed to keep strict discipline—suddenly, they’re a lot tougher than they meant to be. Or a manager under the gun to hit targets—maybe they start overlooking things they shouldn’t. Even a group of friends can find themselves going along with stuff they’d never do alone, just because they want to fit in.
Now, you might think, “If you’ve got strong character, you can resist that kind of pressure.” But here’s something to really pay attention to—most of us are more influenced by our surroundings than we like to admit.
The real key is learning to spot when the situation is nudging you in the wrong direction, and figuring out how to push back. That could mean speaking up, looking for support, or sometimes, just stepping away.
By paying close attention to the environment you’re in, you’ve got a better shot at making choices that actually reflect your real values—even when it’s tough.
